Recursive Self-Improvement of Predicates for Skill Routing via Minimum
Bayes Risk Replay and Held-out Gates
Anonymous ACL submission
Abstract
001
As agents are expected to solve broader and
002
more complex tasks, they rely on external
003
knowledge saved as skills to handle tasks be-
004
yond the LLM’s parametric capabilities. As the
005
skill corpora grows into hundreds or thousands
006
of skills, skill routing becomes a bottleneck,
007
where the agent must efficiently retrieve and
008
select the appropriate skills to complete a task.
009
Recent skill routing approaches leverage task
010
feedback to improve skill routing performance
011
online. However, feedback-driven updates to
012
routing criteria can regress performance, and
013
accumulating task feedback at scale requires ef-
014
ficient experience management. We introduce
015
a recursive self-improving algorithm for skill
016
routing in a black-box setting called RouterBSI.
017
It refines task applicability predicates using
018
Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) with bounded
019
replay to minimize errors on seen tasks and a
020
held-out validation gate to reduce regressions
021
on unseen tasks. The router evaluates pred-
022
icates for top-k retrieved skills then selects
023
skills if the task satisfies their respective pred-
024
icate. RouterBSI improves its cold-start top-5
025
recall of required skills by 24.9% across differ-
026
ent retrievers on tasks from TheoremQA, Log-
027
icBench, ToolQA, MedCalc-Bench, CHAMP,
028
and BigCodeBench sharing a 26k skill corpus.
029
On average, it retains 90.5% of the required
030
skills in top 5 from the top 50 skills retrieved.
031
1
Introduction
032
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly
033
rely on reusable skills to extend their capabilities
034
beyond knowledge encoded in model parameters.
035
These skills package procedural knowledge that
036
can be reused across recurring classes of tasks. As
037
skill libraries grow, however, explicitly exposing
038
every available skill in the context becomes increas-
039
ingly impractical. Recent work therefore shifts to-
040
ward Skill Retrieval Augmentation (SRA), where
041
skills must be retrieved and loaded from a large-
042
scale skill corpora (Su et al., 2026) (Figure 1).
043

In SRA, retrieval based on semantic relevance
044
alone is not enough. Skills must be invoked based
045
on their downstream utility for completing a task to
046
reliably augment the agent’s capabilities. Current
047
agents can struggle to distinguish useful skills from
048
irrelevant ones even when the correct skill has been
049
successfully retrieved (Su et al., 2026). We refer to
050
skill routing as the process of determining which
051
retrieved candidate skills are applicable to a task
052
and should therefore enter the agent's active con-
053
text for completing a task. Reliable routing must
054
distinguish applicability from semantic relatedness:
055
a skill can be topically similar to a task without
056
satisfying the requirements under which its proce-
057
dure should be invoked. This distinction becomes
058
increasingly important as broader candidate sets
059
introduce irrelevant procedures that can distract the
060
model or interfere with downstream reasoning.
061
Existing routing approaches address this prob-
062
lem through similarity scores, learned utility func-
063
tions, direct model-based selection, and explicit
064
activation conditions.
Learned retrievers and
065
rerankers can improve discrimination among can-
066
didates but encode routing criteria implicitly in
067
model parameters and require additional optimiza-
068
tion data and compute. In contrast, non-parametric
069
approaches keep the underlying model fixed while
070
modifying external state that influences future de-
071
cisions. Yet persistent external updates introduce
072
a different reliability problem. An edit motivated
073
1

by a failure can correct similar failure cases while
074
undoing corrections to previously handled tasks or
075
degrading performance on other cases. As interac-
076
tion histories grow, retaining all prior examples for
077
checking each update also makes continual adap-
078
tation increasingly expensive. This creates a need
079
for a routing mechanism whose applicability cri-
080
teria are explicit and editable, but whose updates
081
are efficiencly constrained by prior experience and
082
independently checked for generalization. These
083
problems of controlling regressions while bound-
084
ing used experience serve as the motivation for our
085
approach.
086
We introduce RouterBSI, a recursive self-
087
improving algorithm for skill routing in a black-box
088
setting called RouterBSI. It refines task applicabil-
089
ity predicates using Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR)
090
with bounded replay to minimize errors on seen
091
tasks and a held-out validation gate to reduce re-
092
gressions on unseen tasks. The router evaluates
093
predicates for top-k retrieved skills then selects
094
skills if the task satisfies their respective predicate.
095
RouterBSI improves its cold-start top-5 recall of
096
required skills by an average of 24.9% across dif-
097
ferent retrievers on tasks from TheoremQA, Log-
098
icBench, ToolQA, MedCalc-Bench, CHAMP, and
099
BigCodeBench sharing a 26k skill corpus. On av-
100
erage, it retains 90.5% of the required skills in top
101
5 from the top 50 skills retrieved. Its top-5 recall
102
is 75.5%, with relative recall improvements over
103
baselines averaging 7.9% to 33.6% across retriev-
104
ers.
105
Our contributions are:
106
• We propose RouterBSI, a non-parametric skill-
107
routing framework that evaluates explicit ap-
108
plicability predicates over retrieved candi-
109
dates, making routing criteria interpretable
110
and directly editable without updating the un-
111
derlying language model.
112
• We develop a recursive self-improvement pro-
113
cedure that refines predicates from routing fail-
114
ures, selects updates through minimum Bayes
115
risk over a bounded replay of relevant and ir-
116
relevant tasks, and rejects updates with higher
117
held-out validation error than the cold-start
118
predicate.
119
• We evaluate RouterBSI on six SRA-Bench
120
datasets with a shared 26K-skill corpus,
121
achieving the highest aggregate nDCG@10
122
and Hit@1 among evaluated methods while
123
ablations establish the contributions of replay
124
and validation.
125
2
Related Works
126
2.1
Non-Parametric Routing Optimization
127
Non-parametric routing optimization updates exter-
128
nal routing state from task feedback while keeping
129
model weights fixed. Experience-based methods
130
revise memories and procedures, but revisions can
131
undo earlier improvements (Wang et al., 2025b;
132
Ouyang et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2024). Structural
133
methods evolve skill relationships, but graph expan-
134
sions can introduce many irrelevant skills, reducing
135
precision or exceeding context limits (Zhang et al.,
136
2025; Bai et al., 2026). Gated updates limit re-
137
gressions through surrogate objectives or rollback
138
criteria but don’t directly minimizing routing error
139
on seen tasks (Mi et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026).
140
Similar to our approach, JTPRO evaluates candi-
141
dates on sampled training minibatches and held-out
142
validation but does not provide bounded experience
143
management for online adaptation (Ghoshal et al.,
144
2026). Retaining earlier routing corrections while
145
bounding experience and evaluation costs remains
146
a challenge. RouterBSI ensures non-decreasing em-
147
pirical error on the retained set while bounding re-
148
play evaluation costs. A held-out gate additionally
149
rejects updates that regress validation performance
150
below the cold-start performance.
151
2.2
Parametric Routing Optimization
152
Parametric routing optimization updates model
153
weights using supervision, preferences, or execu-
154
tion feedback. Learned retrievers and rerankers
155
score relevance or utility of skill for task (Qin et al.,
156
2024; Zheng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Li
157
et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026), while direct selec-
158
tors predict which capability to invoke or whether
159
invocation is needed (Wang et al., 2025a; Qian
160
et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). Reinforcement-
161
learning policies optimize skill routing from down-
162
stream rewards (Wang et al., 2026b; Xia et al.,
163
2026a; Zhang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Wu
164
et al., 2026). These approaches require large train-
165
ing data and encode routing criteria implicitly in
166
model weights. RouterBSI keeps the model fixed
167
and refines natural-language applicability predi-
168
cates that humans can inspect and edit.

2.3
Static Routing Without Feedback-driven
170
Optimization
171
Static routing uses retrieval or inference-time selec-
172
tion without persistently optimizing routing criteria
173
from task feedback. Similarity methods retrieve
174
skills through semantic or lexical matching (Wang
175
et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026),
176
while structured methods organize search through
177
predefined hierarchies or relationships (Li et al.,
178
2026a; Sun et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Packer
179
et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025).
180
LLM-based methods select or compose capabili-
181
ties at inference time (Chen et al., 2026b; Xia et al.,
182
2026b; Shen et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). These
183
approaches support skill routing but do not convert
184
failures into persistent corrections. RouterBSI uses
185
routing failures to refine applicability predicates
186
online in a black-box setting.
187
3
Problem Definition
188
We study recursive self-improvement for skill rout-
189
ing, where an agent updates skill applicability pred-
190
icates from routing failures while avoiding regres-
191
sions. Each skill s from skill library S has a predi-
192
cate ps(q) = {True or False} indicating whether
193
it should be selected for task q. A routing failure
194
occurs when this prediction disagrees with whether
195
s from predicted skills Pq is in ground-truth set
196
of required skills Gq, producing either a missing
197
required skill or a selected irrelevant skill. Since
198
S is a large library of skills, we only evaluate the
199
predicates from skills in the top k based on retrieval
200
score r(q, Ks) between task q and the skill key Ks.
201
Given a failure in top k skills sk, the objective is
202
to iteratively update the affected predicate psk(q)
203
to correct the observed error without degrading
204
previously learned or unseen routing decisions.
205

Method
206
4.1
Predicate-Based Skill Routing
207
Skills are selected according to whether the task
208
aligns with the type of task each skill is intended
209
to handle. This is determined by evaluating the
210
skill’s predicate statement for the given task. The
211
predicate evaluates to true when the task aligns
212
with the intended task type and to false otherwise.
213
The router first retrieves the top-k skills based
214
on the retrieval score r(q, Ks) between task q and
215
the skill key Ks. Given task q, it then evaluates the
216
predicate psk of each retrieved skill sk, where sk ∈
217
S@k, to determine whether it holds for q: psk(q) =
218
{True or False}. The router selects skills whose

5
Experiments
272
5.1
Benchmarks and Skill Corpus.
273
We conduct experiments on SRA-Bench, which
274
comprises six capability-intensive benchmarks:
275
TheoremQA (Chen et al., 2023), LogicBench (Par-
276
mar et al., 2024),
ToolQA (Zhuang et al.,
277
2023), CHAMP (Mao et al., 2024), MedCalc-
278
Bench (Khandekar et al., 2024),
and Big-
279
CodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2025). These datasets
280
cover diverse task settings, including mathematical
281
reasoning, formal logic, tool use, and code genera-
282
tion. Each instance is paired with annotated gold
283
skill(s) and evaluated against a shared external skill
284
corpus, enabling decomposed analysis of retrieval,
285
incorporation, and end-task execution. We split
286
each dataset into train, validation, and test splits
287
with ratios of 70%, 15%, 15%, respectively. To
288
evaluate the learning capabilities of baselines, we
289
further filter and balance splits such that each split
290
has at least one task that share the same required
291
skill.

5.2
Evaluation Metrics.
293
We evaluate skill routing and downstream perfor-
294
mance conditioned on the selected skills. For skill
295
routing, we report Recall@k and nDCG@k. We
296
additionally report F1@k to compare filtering ca-
297
pabilities. We also report retention as Ret@k to
298
compare the percentage of required skills retained
299
in top k from the retrieved skills. For downstream
300
performance, each benchmark follows its standard
301
evaluation protocol to measure success rate: rule-
302
based exact match or accuracy for reasoning and
303
QA datasets, and pass@1 based on unit-test exe-
304
cution for BigCodeBench. Averages are measured
305
across task instances.
306
5.3
Selected Models.
307
We evaluate five models spanning four open-weight
308
checkpoints and one proprietary frontier model:
309
Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Qwen3.8-27B
310
(Qwen Team, 2026b), Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct
311
(Meta, 2024), gpt-oss-120b (OpenAI, 2025), and
312
GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026).

5.4
Baselines
314
We study retrieval, reranker, and selection base-
315
lines. The retrievers include sparse and dense re-
316
trievers (Su et al., 2026) and SkillSight, a hybrid
317
retriever. They are trained on training split and
318
frozen on validation and test splits. LLM Select is
319
a static router, and LLM Direct and LLM Oracle
320
are downstream performance baselines represent-
321
ing without skills and with ground-truth skill set,
322
respectively (Su et al., 2026). The non-parametric
323
optimization baselines are SkillDag and Skill-Pro
324
(Mi et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026). RouterBSIinit
325
and RouterBSI refer to the cold-start and final
326
iteration performance.
RouterBSIstrict selects
327
skills only when their predicate evaluates to true.
328
RouterBSItopk are the top k skills using the sum
329
of their predicate label and the retrieval score.

5.5
Implementation Details.
331
The retrievers use either pretrained embedding
332
models and/or lexical matching, so they do not re-
333
quire training. Candidate skills are retrieved from
334
the shared external skill corpus in response to the
335
input query. The skill routing baselines are condi-
336
tioned on the top 50 retrieved skills and use some
337
optimization method to improve performance. The
338
exception is SkillDAG where it first retrieves top 5
339
skills then expands them until reaching top k. Its
340
skills are ranked based on graph depth from top 5
341
retrieved skills and retrieval score. SkillSight is the
342
default retriever. Qwen3.5-4B is the default model
343
used in our experiments. The non-parametric base-
344
lines, including ours, do not output a continuous
345
score like rerankers, so we rank them by the sum
346
of their binary label and the retrieval score, where
347
1 is the label for selected skills and 0 otherwise.
348
We use a temperature of 1 for proposing candi-
349
date predicates and 0 for evaluating predicates and
350
downstream performance. RouterBSI is optimized
351
for 10 iterations. In downstream tasks, we use k
352
= 5 skills for SkillRouter and RouterBSItopk, and
353
we set k = 10 for SkillDAG because k = 5 would
354
match the retriever’s performance.

Required Skill Retention
374

tion converges on the training data and improves
